Past medical history is unremarkable. He reports heavy alcohol consumption for the past several years but says he quit recently. On physical examination, the patient appears jaundiced and is ill-appearing. There is shifting dullness presents on abdominal percussion with a positive fluid wave. Sclera are icteric. Bilateral gynecomastia is present. Laboratory findings are significant for the following:
Hgb 13 g/dL  
Leukocyte count 4,500/mm3  
Platelets 86,000/mm3  
Aspartate transaminase (AST) 108 U/L  
Alanine transaminase (ALT) 55 U/L  
GGT 185 U/L  
Urea 23 mg/dL  
Iron 120 μg/dL  
Ferritin 180 μg/dL  
Transferrin saturation 40%

A 65-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for fatigue. The patient states that he has not been sleeping well and requests sleep medication to help him with his fatigue. He recently changed his diet to try to increase his energy and has been on a vegetarian diet for the past several months. The patient has no significant past medical history. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day and drinks 5 alcoholic beverages per day. The patient has lost 12 pounds since his last visit 1 month ago. Physical exam demonstrates a tired man. He appears thin, and his skin and sclera are icteric. Abdominal ultrasound is notable for a thin-walled and enlarged gallbladder. A urine sample is collected and is noted to be amber in color.

A 61-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of pain and redness of both eyes. He has new blurry vision and difficulty opening his eyes in bright surroundings. He has not had any recent trauma. He uses contact lenses daily. He had surgery on his left eye 6 months ago after a penetrative trauma caused by a splinter. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows congestion of the perilimbal conjunctivae bilaterally. Visual acuity is decreased bilaterally. Ocular movements are normal. Slit-lamp examination shows a cornea with normal contours and leukocytes in the anterior chambers of both eyes. The eyelids, eyelashes, and lacrimal ducts show no abnormalities.

A 29-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her father because of a change in her behavior over the past 8 months. The father says that his daughter has become increasingly withdrawn; she has not answered any phone calls or visited her family and friends. The patient says that she has to stay at home because a foreign intelligence service is monitoring her. She thinks that they are using a magnetic field to read her mind. Mental status exam shows disjointed and perseverative thinking. She is anxious and has a flat affect.

A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for 2 years. The patient also reports monthly episodes of pelvic and back pain accompanied by painful diarrhea for 6 years. She takes naproxen for the pain, which has provided some relief. Menses have occurred at regular 28-day intervals since menarche at the age of 11 years and last for 7 days. She is sexually active with her husband and does not use contraception. Pelvic and rectal examination shows no abnormalities. A hysterosalpingogram is unremarkable.
gt_diagnosis: Endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity

case_vignette: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommates for aggressive and unusual behavior. His roommates state that he has been under a lot of stress lately from his final exams and has been more reclusive. They state that this evening he was very irritable and was yelling at his computer prior to breaking it, followed by him spending several hours at the gym. His temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 137/98 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 23/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for an irritable young man. Cardiopulmonary exam is notable for tachycardia and bilateral clear breath sounds. Neurological exam reveals dilated pupils. The patient is notably diaphoretic and speaks very rapidly during the physical exam and is aggressive. He is given haloperidol, diphenhydramine, and diazepam for sedation and placed in soft restraints. His symptoms resolved over the next 10 hours in the emergency department.

A 25-year-old man is in the middle of an ascent up a mountain, at an elevation of about 4,500 meters. This is the 4th day of his expedition. His friend notices that in the last few hours, he has been coughing frequently and appears to be short of breath. He has used his albuterol inhaler twice in the past 4 hours, but it does not seem to help. Within the past hour, he has coughed up some frothy, slightly pink sputum and is now complaining of nausea and headache. Other than his asthma, which has been well-controlled on a steroid inhaler, he is healthy.

A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of worsening shortness of breath, cough, and a 4-kg (8.8-lb) weight loss over the last year. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, and pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. Physical examination shows decreased breath sounds. A flow-volume loop obtained via pulmonary function testing is shown.

A 78-year-old man presented with painful swelling and ulceration of the glans penis of 1 month's duration. His medical history included an elevated white blood cell count and inguinal lymphadenopathy discovered 9 years prior. Four years after initial presentation, he experienced fatigue, weight loss, and loss of appetite. The current illness began 1 month prior to admission when he noticed asymptomatic 'green-yellow welts' and swelling of the glans penis. The swelling became progressively painful and evolved to the size of an 'orange' over 4 days. Previous treatments with topical antibiotics, antifungal agents, hydrogen peroxide soaks, warm compresses, and cephalexin showed no improvement.

Physical Examination: Patient appeared healthy. The glans penis and corona were grossly edematous, with a 3.7 × 3.3-cm tender, firm ulcer on the ventral surface of the penis with overlying black eschar, adherent yellow crust, and granulation tissue. No urethral discharge was present.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory Tests: Routine blood test results were within normal limits. Cultures, assays, and blood tests evaluating for viral, bacterial, or fungal etiology were negative.

- Pathology Studies: Biopsy of the glans penis ulcer showed dermal infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes, which were CD20+, CD79a+, and CD5+, within the background of a reactive T-cell infiltrate. PCR analysis revealed a clonal IgH gene rearrangement.

- Imaging Studies: PET-CT scan demonstrated FDG-avid abdominal and peripancreatic lymph nodes.
  Image Title: Clinical Appearance of the Penis
  Image Description: Grossly edematous glans penis and corona with a tender, firm ulcer on the ventral surface of the penis with overlying black eschar, adherent yellow crust, and granulation tissue.

  Image Title: Histologic Evaluation of Penile Lesion
  Image Description: Hematoxylin-eosin staining showing dermal infiltrate of large, atypical lymphocytes within a reactive T-cell infiltrate (original magnification ×100)
gt_diagnosis: Richter's transformation presenting as penile ulcer (transformation of chronic lymphocytic leukemia to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)

Physical Examination: - Uncorrected visual acuity measured 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS- Pupils were symmetric, with no relative afferent pupillary defect- Initial anterior segment examination was normal with absence of cataract- Initial dilated fundus examination showed no apparent abnormalities in either eye- At 2 weeks: central macular thickening in fundus examination- At 7 weeks: mild posterior subcapsular cataract visible in right eye

Diagnostic Tests: Spectral-domain OCT findings:- Initial examination (4 days post-injury):   Image Description: Preserved foveal contour in both eyes without cystoid abnormalities. Right eye showed subtle irregularity of the outer retinal layers, most notable nasal to the fovea  - Two weeks post-injury:  Image Description: Intraretinal cystoid changes and subfoveal ellipsoid zone disruption in the right eye  - Seven weeks post-injury:  Image Description: Restoration of foveal contour with decreased cystoid abnormalities, small subfoveal hyporeflective space, and further loss of outer retinal layers in the nasal macula  - Four months post-injury:  Image Description: Persistent subfoveal hyporeflective space in the inner retina with interval restoration of subfoveal outer retinal structures
gt_diagnosis: Lightning-induced retinopathy with delayed-onset cystoid macular abnormalities

case_vignette:
A 40-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain and constipation. She had been evaluated 3 months earlier for 3-4 months of amenorrhea. She had a history of thyroid condition. During the previous evaluation, thyroid-stimulating hormone was undetectable, and she was prescribed methimazole. She continued to have amenorrhea and reported abdominal fullness and constipation.

Physical Examination: Vital signs were unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a tender midline abdominal mass.

Diagnostic Tests: - Initial Tests:    * Point-of-care (POC) urine human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) test: negative    * Thyroid-stimulating hormone: undetectable    * Radioiodine thyroid uptake study was performed      - Follow-up Tests:    * Serum hCG: 74,503 mIU/mL    * Ultrasonography: Confirmed live intrauterine pregnancy at 24 weeks

A 6-year-old Hispanic girl presented with fevers, extremity pain, and joint stiffness. Initial symptoms began with decreased mobility and pain, followed by development of numerous hypopigmented atrophic sclerotic plaques diffusely on the face, trunk, and extremities approximately 2 years after initial presentation. There was sparing of the hands and feet, an absence of Raynaud phenomenon, and no internal organ involvement.

Physical Examination: Physical examination revealed decreased range of motion of the shoulders, elbows, wrists, knees, and fingers without sclerodactyly or other signs of cutaneous involvement.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests:    - Eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count: 3500/uL)    - Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (108 mm/hr)    - Hypergammaglobulinemia (IgG level: 5725 mg/dL)    - Positive antinuclear antibody (>1:2560, speckled)    - Negative anti–Scl-70 antibodies  - Imaging studies:    - MRI of left forearm showed diffuse thickening and edema of the musculature  - Pathological examination:    - Histopathologic analysis revealed mononuclear, plasmacytic, and eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate invading the fascia, fat, and muscle

A woman in her 50s presented with unilateral eye irritation. She had recently been prescribed chloramphenicol drops for suspected bacterial conjunctivitis. She stored her antibiotic drops beside her EC refill liquid in her bathroom cupboard and mistakenly administered the EC fluid to her eye, resulting in instant ocular pain, redness, and blurred vision. She irrigated her eye as soon as she realized her mistake.

Physical Examination: There was superficial punctate staining on the cornea but no epithelial defect.

Diagnostic Tests: - pH Testing:    - EC liquid pH: 6    - Ocular pH: 7
gt_diagnosis: Mild ocular chemical injury due to electronic cigarette liquid exposure

case_vignette:
A woman in her 60s with stage IV adenocarcinoma of the lungs presented with a large ulceration in the right temporal region. She reported unilateral headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and blurred vision affecting her right eye. All symptoms occurred 2 weeks after the first infusion of nivolumab, which was initiated after failure of combined chemotherapy with vinorelbine and cisplatin. Six weeks later, while still receiving nivolumab therapy, a slowly enlarging skin necrosis appeared on her right temple.

Physical Examination: The right temporal artery was palpable and extremely tender.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests: Blood test results showed substantially elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels.- Pathological examination: Temporal artery biopsy results revealed characteristic histopathological features with intimal thickening, luminal stenosis, and dense inflammatory cell infiltrates.- Imaging:  Image Title: Clinical Findings at First Presentation  Image Description: The large ulceration is located in the right temporal region of the scalp.  Image Title: Temporal Artery Biopsy Results  Image Description: Histopathological results show intimal thickening and luminal stenosis of the temporal artery, as well as the presence of dense granulomatous inflammatory cell infiltrates (original magnification ×100; hematoxylin-eosin stain).

A patient in their 70s presented to the emergency department with chest tightness and shortness of breath for 5 hours and loss of consciousness for 10 minutes. The patient's medical history included metastatic rectal cancer and hypertension.

Physical Examination: Temperature: 36.0°CBlood pressure: 52/26 mm HgPulse rate: 45 beats per minute Respiratory rate: 6 breaths per minuteExamination revealed ecchymosis on the lower limbsCardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory Tests:  * N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide: 6770 ng/L (reference: 300-900 ng/L)  * Troponin I: normal  * Serum potassium: 9.37 mEq/L (reference: 3.5-5.3 mEq/L)  * Serum creatinine: 7.2 mg/dL (reference: 0.7-1.2 mg/dL)  * Serum uric acid: 13,176.5 mg/dL (reference: 3495.7-8504.2 mg/dL)- ECG Findings:  Image Title: Initial ECG  Image Description: Coved ST-segment elevation of 4 mm with downsloping ST segment and T-wave inversion in lead V1. Tall peaked and narrow-based T waves, loss of P waves, and prolonged QRS duration (210 milliseconds)    Image Title: Repeated ECG  Image Description: Significant increases in the amplitude of T waves in leads V2 through V6, further prolonged QRS duration

case_vignette:
A 49-year-old woman presented with healed ulcers of the lower lip and nasal dorsum and a nonhealing ulcer of the left lateral infraorbital area. She reported several years of facial ulcers described as 'scratches' developing over weeks to months into red, indurated, tender ulcers that finally crusted and healed. Review of systems was positive for dry mouth, Raynaud phenomenon, morning joint pain, mild hand and ankle swelling, and dysphagia.

Physical Examination: Examination revealed:- Healed ulcers on lower lip and nasal dorsum- Nonhealing ulcer in left lateral infraorbital area- Later developed:  - Diplopia  - Sense of fullness below left eye  - Restriction of left eye into hypotropic and exotropic position  - Full-thickness defect through lateral lower eyelid  - Exposed conjunctiva and bony orbital rim

Diagnostic Tests: Laboratory Tests:- Positive antinuclear antibodies (titer 1:360; nuclear and cytoplasmic staining)- Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level (78 U/L)- Decreased C4 complement level- Normal results for multiple other tests including anti-proteinase 3, antimyeloperoxidase, anti-Scl-70, HIV, antiphospholipid, C3 complement and othersImaging Studies:- Maxillofacial CT findings:  - Nasal septal perforation  - Saddle nose deformity  - Clear paranasal sinuses  - Left infraorbital soft-tissue defect- MRI findings:  - Amorphous mass of hypointense material in inferior and temporal orbitPathology:- Initial biopsy: Granulomatous inflammation- Orbital biopsies: Foreign-body granulomas with polarizable material- Cultures: Negative for infectious causesImages:1. Title: Clinical Appearance of the Patient   Description: Shows saddle nose deformity and infraorbital ulcer at onset of diplopia2. Title: Histologic Evaluation of the Nonhealing Ulcer   Description: Biopsy tissue showing acellular, eosinophilic foreign material with surrounding inflammation, including foreign-body granulomas
gt_diagnosis: Autoimmune/inflammatory syndrome induced by adjuvants (ASIA) due to poly-l-lactic acid dermal filler

case_vignette:
A 78-year-old woman with no prior medical history, including no autoimmune disease. In February 2010, she was diagnosed with a stage IIA melanoma on the left leg (Breslow thickness, 2.5 mm; no ulceration, negative sentinel lymph node). In June 2019, she developed an iliac lymph node metastasis. After lymph node dissection, she received nivolumab treatment from September 2019 to September 2020. In February 2021, she presented with marked skin thickening and painful swelling of the limbs.

Physical Examination: Patient presented with painful cutaneous sclerosis on the limbs, flanks, and abdomen (pain visual analog scale: 8 of 10; Rodnan score: 33 of 51). Multiple plaque-type lesions with ulcerated areas were observed. Physical examination revealed skin thickening.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory Tests:    * Blood tests showed eosinophilia (1200/mm3)    * Autoantibody panel was negative    * Cytokines assay showed:      - TNF-α: 30.1 pg/mL (normal <10.85 pg/mL)      - IL-8: 30 pg/mL (normal <28.75 pg/mL)      - IL-6: 10.3 pg/mL (normal <5.96 pg/mL)  - Imaging Studies:    * PET scan showed no signs of fasciitis    * CT scan revealed an unresectable iliac lymph node without distant metastasis  - Pathological Examination:    * First skin biopsy: Showed histiocytic and neutrophilic reticular dermal infiltrate with slight edema    * Second skin biopsy: Revealed thickening of upper dermis with broad sclerotic collagen bundles in horizontal pattern, lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate, and neutrophils diffusing within collagen bundles. Blood vessel linings were thickened and hyalinized.

A man in his 80s with a history of asthma and bronchiectasis who was receiving immunosuppression therapy (methylprednisolone, 12 mg every other day) presented with dyspnea and right arm swelling and tenderness 8 days before transfer. Medical history included cerebrovascular accident, atrial flutter, and aortic stenosis.

Physical Examination: Vital signs were stable. Patient had edema of the right arm, hand, and fingers with overlying diffuse violaceous nonblanching and edematous nodules. Purpuric plaques were noted on the right cheek, central chest, left arm, and left posterior shoulder.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory findings:     - Hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL (reference range 13.5-17.5 g/dL)    - Blood cultures showed 'yeast' at time of transfer      - Imaging studies:    - CT chest showed diffusely scattered patchy lung infiltrates suspicious for inflammatory disease or infection, along with a small left pleural effusion      - Pathology:    - Skin biopsy from purpuric plaque    Image Title: Clinical photograph of right arm and hand    Image Description: Shows edematous right arm and hand with violaceous nodules        Image Title: Biopsy specimen photomicrograph (H&E stain)    Image Description: Shows unremarkable epidermis overlying diffuse transdermal edema and hemorrhage. Diffuse, patchy basophilic infiltrate with lymphohistiocytic inflammation and abundant infectious organisms in dermis        Image Title: Oil-immersion photomicrograph    Image Description: Shows sporangia, spores, and morulalike forms        Image Title: Wet mount of cultured organisms    Image Description: Shows sporangia, spores, and scattered morulalike forms

A patient in their 60s presented to the emergency department with paroxysmal chest pain. The chest pain had occurred 5 times during the day, and each episode lasted 15 to 30 minutes.

Physical Examination: On arrival, the patient's blood pressure and pulse rate were 106/52 mm Hg and 64 beats per minutes, respectively. Chest auscultation revealed normal breath and heart sounds with no murmurs.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory Tests:
  • Hemogram, serum electrolyte levels, kidney and liver function tests, B-type natriuretic peptide and D-dimer levels were all within normal limits
  • Cardiac troponin I level was 25 ng/mL (normal, <0.023 ng/mL)

- ECG Findings:
  Image A Title: Initial ECG
  Image A Description: Revealed sinus rhythm, ST-segment elevation in leads III and aVR, Q wave in lead III, and ST-segment depression in leads I, II, aVL, aVF, and V2 to V6

  Image B Title: Repeated ECG (taken during recurrent chest pain on second day)
  Image B Description: Reveals sinus bradycardia (46 beats per minute), Q-wave amplitude deepening, ST-segment falling back to equipotential line, and T-wave inversion in lead III

- Coronary Angiography:
  Findings showed total occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA) and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery (LMCA)
gt_diagnosis: Acute non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) with Aslanger pattern

case_vignette:
A 1-year-old child with chronic right middle ear effusion presented following resolution of the third episode of pneumococcal meningitis. Prior immunological workup yielded normal findings. The patient failed a distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) newborn hearing screen on the right side and passed on the left side. Auditory brainstem response (ABR) testing had not been performed due to poor parental compliance.

Physical Examination: Clear fluid pulsated from the middle ear space after myringotomy on the right side. Middle ear exploration showed clear fluid coming from the round window niche and the oval window. A large congenital dehiscence was noted in the stapes footplate. CSF was noted to be pulsating through the footplate. A fistula was noted through a patent round window.

Diagnostic Tests: - Imaging Studies:    - MRI: No evidence of encephalocele, meningocele, or calvarial defect    - CT scan: No evidence of bony dehiscence, ossicles appeared present and grossly normal. Identified malformed cochleae (right more severe), middle ear effusion on right side, and enlarged vestibular aqueduct on left side.      Image Title: Computed Tomographic Image Without Contrast      Image Description: A) Coronal view of right temporal bone showing middle ear opacification, cochlea dysplasia, and no evidence of tegmen defect. B) Axial view showing malformed cochlear and vestibular dysplasia.        - Auditory Tests:      - Initial ABR: Moderate sensorineural hearing loss on left side and severe sensorineural hearing loss on right      - Follow-up ABR (1 year post-surgery): Mild sensorineural hearing loss on left side and severe sensorineural hearing loss on right
gt_diagnosis: Synchronous cerebrospinal fluid fistulae through the oval and round windows

case_vignette:
A man in his 40s with unilateral otomandibular syndrome (OMS) associated with severe temporal bone hypoplasia had undergone many mandibular and auricular reconstruction surgeries in childhood. He presented with a history of deep unilateral neck cellulitis. The first episode occurred in 2014 with no obvious cause. The second episode occurred in 2021, with discharge through the artificial ear canal. Two months after the second episode, the patient experienced another recurrence of neck cellulitis.

Physical Examination: Discharge was noted through the artificial ear canal during the second episode of cellulitis.

Diagnostic Tests: - Imaging Studies:    1. Initial CT scan:       - Title: Axial Plane CT Scan       - Description: Showed collection in the right parapharyngeal space and neck collection. A hypodense lesion was noted in the middle ear.        2. Follow-up MRI and CT scan:       - Title: Contrast-Enhanced Coronal Plane MRI       - Description: Revealed a fistula originating from the middle ear       - Title: Axial plane diffusion-weighted MRI       - Description: Showed a hyperintense 23-mm lesion at the edge of the petrous bone        3. Surgical Findings:       - 2-centimeter mass found during drilling of the hypoplastic petrous bone       - Millimetric fistula at the tip of the mastoid running into the sternocleidomastoid muscle
gt_diagnosis: Congenital cholesteatoma with fistula formation in the setting of otomandibular syndrome

case_vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with recurrent requirement of ventilation tube insertion in both ears. Past medical history was not specifically mentioned.

Physical Examination: Otoscopy showed a retracted tympanic membrane and attic destruction in the right ear and effusion in the left ear. Nasopharyngoscopy showed narrow ET orifices on both sides. Neither ear responded to the Valsalva maneuver or inflation-deflation test. Audiometry showed bilateral mixed hearing loss.

Diagnostic Tests: - Initial Imaging:    Image Title: Preoperative contrast-enhanced CT    Image Description: No remarkable abnormal finding      - Follow-up Imaging (16 months later):    Image Title: Postoperative contrast-enhanced CT    Image Description: Soft tissue mass, sized approximately 2 cm, with mild enhancement at the left Rosenmuller fossa        Image Title: MRI Findings    Image Description:     - T1-weighted: Lesion with high signal intensity at the Rosenmuller fossa    - T2-weighted: Lesion with high signal intensity at the Rosenmuller fossa    - Gadolinium-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted: Lesion with high signal intensity and no definite enhancement      - Endoscopic Findings:    Image Title: Endoscopic View of the Left Nasopharynx    Image Description: Bulging lesion on the medial side of the torus tubarius

case_vignette:
A healthy, immunocompetent 30-year-old man undergoing basic military training presented with a 4-day history of a progressive vesiculopustular eruption of the anterior neck and chin. The patient denied symptoms of pruritus, burning, or fever at time of presentation. He had not received the smallpox vaccination but had engaged in simulated unarmed combat with individuals who had recently been vaccinated. Medical history was noncontributory, and the patient was not taking any medications. During hospitalization, the patient developed fevers to 39°C, progressive edema of the face, and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy.

Physical Examination: More than 2 dozen monomorphic, broad-based folliculocentric pustules with central umbilication, overlying serum crust, and surrounding erythema and edema of the anterior neck, chin, and inferior cheeks.

Diagnostic Tests: - Histopathologic examination (Punch biopsy):     - Demonstrated viral changes to the epidermis with ballooning degeneration of keratinocytes with intracytoplasmic inclusions (Guarnieri bodies) and a brisk lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate    - PCR Test:    - Confirmed presence of vaccinia virus      - Electron Microscopy:    - Demonstrated viral particles within the Guarnieri bodies      - Images:    Figure 1 Title: Clinical Findings    Description: Vesiculopustules with central umbilication in the beard area at time of presentation        Figure 2 Title: Histopathologic Findings From Lesional Skin of the Right Cheek    Description: Shows epidermal necrosis, intraepidermal edema, ballooning degeneration, necrotic keratinocytes, neutrophilic infiltrate, and Guarnieri bodies within keratinocytes

He was treated by an outside physician with multiple courses of antibiotics and steroids, with marginal improvement.

Physical Examination: There were no overt findings on physical examination.

Diagnostic Tests: - Imaging studies:    1. Initial CT scan of neck:       Image Title: Computed Tomographic Images of the Neck Examining the Right Parapharyngeal Space       Image Description: Shows calcification in the right parapharyngeal space        2. Magnetic resonance angiography of the neck: unremarkable        3. Surgical exploration findings:       - Initial intraoral exploration: no findings       - Transcervical exploration: 7-mm bony mass located along the course of the expected stylomandibular ligament above the digastric tendon        4. Pathology:       Finding: Benign bone with associated fibroconnective tissue

case_vignette:
A 26-year-old man presented with a several-year history of persistent round lesions with a scar-like appearance on his face. His condition had previously been diagnosed and treated unsuccessfully. He denied experiencing previous inflammation and had no history of chicken pox, acne or traumatic lesions in those areas.

Physical Examination: Several round atrophic lesions on his face, symmetric and bilateral, located especially on the malar and preauricular areas, with a diameter of 5 to 10 mm. The skin lesions were not indurated and displayed no epidermal changes.

Diagnostic Tests: - Histopathologic examination:     - Showed significant epidermal dell and superficial dermal lymphocytic infiltrate associated with dermal fibrosis    - Orcein stain demonstrated reduction of elastic fibers in the dermis beneath the epidermal dell  Images:  - Figure 1:    Title: Atrophic lesions on the patient    Description: Shows atrophic lesions on the patient's left cheek (A) and with a cicatricial appearance on the preauricular right area (B)    - Figure 2:    Title: Histological examination    Description: A) Panoramic histological view shows slight depression of the epidermis (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification, ×2)    B) Orcein staining shows reduction in elastic fibers beside lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate compared with surrounding healthy area (orcein; original magnification, ×10)

She had no medical history and was only taking over-the-counter vitamin supplements. She was previously at her baseline functional status until 2 months ago when symptoms began progressing.

case_vignette:
A man in his 70s presented with a persistent eruption of 5 years' duration. He had been treated with oral methotrexate for presumed chronic dermatitis after treatments with oral antibiotics, oral doxepin, and UV-B phototherapy had failed. Investigation of medical records revealed a history of HSV-2 infection on the buttocks prior to the development of the current eruption at the same site.

Physical Examination: Multiple erythematous and violaceous plaques and nodules clustered on the superior buttocks and intergluteal cleft bilaterally. The lesions were smooth and firm.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests: Syphilis screen results were negative. Molecular analysis of the T-cell receptor gamma gene showed a weak clonal band in a polyclonal background. Repeat molecular studies showed no evidence of clonal rearrangement.- Pathological findings:  First biopsy: Dense infiltrate of atypical CD4+ small to medium-sized lymphocytes in the upper dermis admixed with eosinophils and plasma cells. Epidermotropism was not identified.  Second biopsy: Similar to prior findings, but with more dense and atypical infiltrate showing epidermotropism.- Images:  Figure 1 Title: Clinical Presentation  Figure 1 Description: Multiple smooth, firm plaques and nodules on the superior buttocks and intergluteal cleft.    Figure 2 Title: Histopathological Findings  Figure 2A Description: Scanning view shows dense infiltrate filling the papillary dermis and extending into the reticular dermis  Figure 2B Description: Higher power shows dense, atypical infiltrate of small to medium-sized lymphocytes
gt_diagnosis: Cutaneous pseudolymphoma arising as Wolf's post-herpetic isotopic response

case_vignette:
A 68-year-old man presented with progressive painless red eye and blurred vision for 2 months. The patient had a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes and a 10-month history of tenosynovitis in his right hand after injury while handling fish, which was refractory to antibiotic treatment.

Physical Examination: Visual acuity was 20/20 OD and counting fingers OS. Conjunctival hyperemia, large yellowish keratic precipitates, 2+ cells, 3+ flare, and 5 mm of hypopyon in the anterior chamber were noted in his left eye. Anterior scleritis was seen in the temporal and inferior areas. Through 1+ vitreous haze, no abnormal changes were found in the fundus. His right eye was normal. Multiple crusted and ulcerated nodules, forming a linear distribution, could be seen in his right hand.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests: Results of laboratory tests were unremarkable. Results of smear and culture of aqueous humor sampled before injection were both negative.- Next-generation sequencing: Sixteen sequence readings of M marinum were detected, accounting for 0.0151% of the genome coverage.- Vitreous culture: Grew mycobacterium, while findings of acid-fast staining of smear were still negative.- Skin biopsy: Pathology showed caseous necrosis.- Images:  Image A Title: Conjunctival hyperemia and hypopyon in the left eye  Image B Title: Nodular lesions in the dorsum of the right hand  Image C Title: Subconjunctival purulent nodules, corneal edema, and hypopyon after treatment in the left eye  Image D Title: Subsided nodular lesions of the right hand after treatment

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory tests:
Serum sodium level: 138 mEq/L
Serum potassium level: 4.4 mEq/L
Serum creatinine level: 0.86 mg/dL

- ECG findings:
Image Title: Figure 1. Electrocardiogram (ECG) at Presentation
Image Description: Regular monomorphic wide complex tachycardia at a rate of 160 beats/min, QRS duration about 180 milliseconds, rS interval of 100 milliseconds in lead V6, predominantly negative complexes in precordial leads

Image Title: Figure 2. Electrocardiogram Showing Transition
Image Description: Shows transition of a narrow to a wide complex tachycardia maintaining the same cycle length

case_vignette:
A man in his 40s with a medical history of factor VII deficiency hemophilia presented with acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Following admission, he was intubated with prone positioning, and treatment was initiated. He was also found to have Staphylococcus hemolyticus bacteremia. Three days after admission, the patient developed erythema and edematous necrotic plaques of the bilateral ears. No devices had been used on the ears. The necrosis progressed during the following days, primarily involving the earlobe of the right ear and a large portion of the helix of the left ear.

Physical Examination: Erythematous plaque (2 cm) with overlying eschar on the right earlobe. Multiple erythematous edematous erosions with eschar and crust on the helical rim of the left ear.

Diagnostic Tests: - Biopsy findings:    Image Title: Hematoxylin-eosin−stained biopsy specimens    Image Description: Detached epidermis with full-thickness necrosis overlying sparse inflammation associated with necrosis of adnexal epithelia, including folliculosebaceous units and eccrine glands. Epidermal and dermal necrosis and ulceration with necrosis of the eccrine glands.

A patient in their early 60s presented with a 2-week history of chest pain during exertion. The chest pain consistently presented during physical activity. The patient was a nonsmoker with no family history of premature coronary artery disease.

Physical Examination: The baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) showed no substantial abnormalities.

Diagnostic Tests: - Stress ECG (Treadmill Test):    - Patient developed left bundle-branch block (LBBB) in stage 2 at heart rate of 107 beats per minute with chest pain    - LBBB resolved following exercise cessation with immediate angina relief    - No ischemic or memory T waves in pre- and post-exercise ECGs        Image Title: ECG Findings of Treadmill Test    Image Description A: Stage 2 treadmill test showing normal sinus rhythm and left bundle-branch block at heart rate of 107 beats per minute    Image Description B: Recovery phase showing normal sinus rhythm and spontaneous disappearance of LBBB        - Coronary computed tomography angiography showed no abnormalities

A 78-year-old woman underwent DMEK surgery. Four weeks after the procedure, mild opacification in the graft-host interface was observed. Visual acuity rehabilitation stopped at 20/50 in the affected eye, although the graft was attached and stromal thickness had returned to normal (552 μm). Six months later, the patient complained about blurred vision.

Physical Examination: Examination revealed:- Graft detachment caused by a paracentral opaque mass- Enlargement of the abnormality - Pseudohypopyon formation- Increased visual impairment at 28 months follow-up

Diagnostic Tests: - Histological Testing:  - Hematoxylin-eosin staining and periodic acid–Schiff staining revealed a detachment of the Descemet graft by a cyst containing cellular debris  - Cytokeratin AE1/AE3 staining was positive  - Chromogen in situ hybridization revealed male donor origin of the cells- Imaging Studies:  Image Title: Slitlamp Findings  Image Description: Shows central opaque area with graft detachment and pseudohypopyon at 9 months post-DMEK  Image Title: Anterior-Segment Optical Coherence Tomography  Image Description: Shows hyperdensity in the area of the graft detachment
gt_diagnosis: Epithelial downgrowth after Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK)

case_vignette:
A man in his 60s with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department with acute chest pain that had begun 30 minutes prior to arrival, which he described as 'an intense pressure radiating to the back.'

Physical Examination: Blood pressure recordings were 150/90 mm Hg and 157/91 mm Hg in his right and left arms, respectively. There was no jugular venous distention or pedal edema.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory Tests:
  • Oxygen saturation: 98% on room air
  • D-dimer level: 6.4 μg/mL (normal value, <0.25 μg/mL)
  • Troponin I level: within normal limits

- ECG Findings:
  Image Title: Electrocardiographic Findings
  Image Description: Initial ECG showed left anterior hemiblock, ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL, and V1 to V6, ST-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF. Prominent J points and J waves in precordial leads. J point in lead V1 higher than R wave. Repeat ECG after 15 minutes showed sinus bradycardia and right bundle-branch block.

- Imaging Studies:
  • Coronary angiography: no abnormal findings
  • Computed tomography angiography of chest: revealed type B aortic intramural hematoma (involving only the descending aorta)

case_vignette:
A young girl presented with a history of chronic, unilateral middle ear effusion that was treated with a pressure equalization (PE) tube by an outside otolaryngologist. She had persistent otorrhea that did not improve with multiple courses of ototopical antibiotics.

Over the years, she developed progressive symptoms of chronic fatigue and joint pain without a definitive diagnosis despite multiple specialist consultations. From 2014 onwards, she experienced recurrent abscesses, indurated erythematous plaques, and sclerosis on both upper legs. She showed no symptoms of autoinflammation or autoimmunity besides periodic fever.

Physical Examination: Clinical examination revealed:- Indurated erythematous plaques and sclerosis on both upper legs- Presence of abscesses on upper legs- No other significant physical findings noted

Diagnostic Tests: Laboratory Tests:- Antinuclear antibodies: negativeImaging Studies:- Magnetic resonance imaging (2019): revealed bilaterally ruptured breast implants- Axillary ultrasound: revealed extensive deposits in multiple axillary lymph nodesPathological Examinations:1. Skin and Muscle Biopsies (Upper legs and abdomen):   - Showed perivascular lymphoplasmacytic inflammation   - Extensive subcutaneous sclerosis of septa and fascia   - Granulomatous inflammation   - Modified oil-red-o (MORO) staining: revealed particles in macrophages with extensive histiocytic reaction and deep fibrosis2. Breast Capsule Pathology:   - Showed extensive accumulation of foamy macrophages3. Axillary Lymph Node Examination:   - Revealed extensive leakage and surrounding inflammation   - No signs of lymphomaImages Referenced:- Figure 1: Clinical images showing abscesses and sclerosis of upper legs- Figure 2: Histopathological images of breast capsule- Figure 3: Various histopathological images showing inflammatory reactions

She developed progressive acute worsening of renal function complicated by pulmonary edema and hyperkalemia refractory to medical therapy (peak creatinine, 4.42; baseline, 1.5). - Normalized blood urea nitrogen
- Persistent anion-gap metabolic acidosis

case_vignette:
A 78-year-old White woman, with a medical history of well-controlled hypothyroidism, presented with a pruritic, erythematous rash for 2 months. The rash began as an annular, erythematous lesion on the left side of her abdomen. One week later, the rash spread to her cheeks and periorbital area. The patient initially experienced mild improvement with oral steroids but had persistent, pruritic macules and papules in a patchy distribution on her face and arms. The rash progressed over the following 3 months, extending into the scalp, neck, legs, and arms with up to 50% skin involvement in these areas. The annular lesions enlarged and exhibited a collarette of scale.

Physical Examination: Pruritic, erythematous rash consisting of annular patches present on:- Face and neck- Bilateral arms- Left leg- VulvaThe lesions showed annular pattern with collarette of scale.

Diagnostic Tests: 1. Laboratory Tests:- Complete blood count: within normal limits- Metabolic panel: within normal limits- Hepatic function: within normal limits- Rapid plasma reagin: within normal limits- Antinuclear antibodies: within normal limits- Patch testing: revealed allergies to cobalt and epoxy resins2. Histologic Findings (punch biopsy of right thigh lesion):- Prominent epidermal acanthosis, alternating with areas of normal epidermal angulation- Superficial and focally deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis- Increased mast cells- Few extravasated erythrocytes- Minor component of plasma cells- Few neutrophils near hair follicles- No significant increase in eosinophils3. Images:- Figure 1: Diffuse erythematous patches and plaques extending across the neck and upper arms- Figure 2: Erythematous papules and plaques on bilateral upper legs- Figure 3: Erythematous plaques with mild collarette of scale on bilateral forearms

case_vignette:
An 83-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin was admitted for a left foot ulcer secondary to vascular disease. During admission, he was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection. Seven days after discharge, the patient consulted again, presenting with new skin lesions consisting of violaceous pretibial lesions with areas of necrosis and intense pain in the right lower limb. The patient had been administered subcutaneous abdominal heparin, with no lesion in the site of injection. No history of cocaine use, fever, dyspnea, chest pain, or other systemic symptoms. No previous hospitalizations or heparin administration.

Physical Examination: Examination revealed pretibial lesions of violaceous coloration, similar to retiform purpura, below the knee, associated with a necrotic lesion in the right calf. Pedal pulse was present, with poorly defined lesions with evolution of the existing ones to limited partial necrosis.

Diagnostic Tests: - Laboratory Tests:    * Platelet count: 173×10⁹/L    * Serum creatinine: 134.37 µmol/L (1.52 mg/dL)    * Glomerular filtration rate: 45.8 mL/min/1.73 m²    * Hemoglobin: 110 g/L    * Leukocytes: 4.75×10⁹/L    * C-reactive protein: 35.8 mg/L    * Autoimmunity studies: negative    * Antiplatelet antibody test: positive for IgG and polivalent antibodies  - Imaging Documentation:    Image Title: Necrotic lesion in the right calf    Image Description: Physical examination showing pretibial lesions of violaceous coloration and necrotic lesion
gt_diagnosis: Skin necrosis induced by low-molecular-weight heparin, produced at a distance from the point of heparin inoculation
